meta.name: DrillGround Drill Resource Packs — promotion_prep_packs payload
meta.description: Paid pack content for the promotion_prep_packs entitlement. Fetched once after that entitlement is granted, then cached. Not a security boundary: see the header of publish-drill-resources.js.

packs.title: Accountability Oral Board Kit — 10 Probes and a Panel Rubric
packs.summary: The candidate brief, ten follow-up probes a real panel would ask in the order they escalate, and the rubric a panel scores against — structure, ownership, specificity, and whether the candidate ever blamed anyone. Plus the self-review sheet for working it alone on video.
packs.removes_prep: The drill needs oral-board question cards and supplies none. The scenario is easy to state; the value is in the follow-up probes, and inventing probes that escalate the way a real panel escalates is exactly what a candidate cannot do for themselves.
packs.local_fill_note: Your department's accountability procedure and its promotional-process format govern. Write your PAR procedure and your board's actual structure — number of panellists, time limit, whether follow-ups are permitted — on the rubric before the first rep.

components.label: Candidate brief and escalating probes
components.instructions: Read the brief once, aloud, then start the clock. Probes are asked in order and only as far as the time allows — a strong candidate reaches probe 7 or 8; a weak one is still on probe 2. Do not help, do not nod, and do not fill silence.

items.text: BRIEF — You are a newly promoted lieutenant. At a working fire last shift, a PAR was called and one of your members did not answer. He turned up ninety seconds later, unharmed, having gone to the rear alone to check a window. Nobody was hurt. Your chief has asked you to talk him through it.
items.teaching_focus: A scenario with no injury, so the candidate cannot hide behind an outcome.

items.text: PROBE 1 — Walk me through what happened, in order.
items.answer: Strong: a clear chronology with times, without editorialising. Weak: starts with the explanation or the excuse before the facts.
items.teaching_focus: Structure before defense.

items.text: PROBE 2 — What was your assignment at the time, and where were you?
items.answer: Strong: states own position plainly, including if it was poor. Weak: vague about own location, which is the first sign of a candidate protecting themselves.
items.teaching_focus: Locating yourself in your own account.

items.text: PROBE 3 — Whose responsibility was it that he was where you did not expect him?
items.answer: Strong: mine. Immediately, without qualification, then the detail. Weak: 'he freelanced' — technically true, and the wrong answer to this question.
items.teaching_focus: The pivot of the whole board. A candidate who does not own this does not recover.

items.text: PROBE 4 — What did you actually say to him, in what words, and when?
items.answer: Strong: specific, prompt, private, and behavior-focused. Weak: 'I had a word with him', which tells the panel nothing happened.
items.teaching_focus: Specificity as evidence that the conversation was real.

items.text: PROBE 5 — He tells you he was checking a window because he thought he saw movement. Does that change your answer?
items.answer: Strong: acknowledges the intent was good and the action was still wrong, and separates the two out loud. Weak: either dismisses it or lets it excuse the breach.
items.teaching_focus: Holding two things at once — good motive, unacceptable act.

items.text: PROBE 6 — What is your responsibility to the other members who saw this happen?
items.answer: Strong: recognizes that an uncorrected breach becomes permission for everyone, and describes what the crew saw and heard afterwards. Weak: treats it as a private matter between two people.
items.teaching_focus: The crew as an audience. Candidates almost always miss this.

items.text: PROBE 7 — This is the second time. What is different about your response?
items.answer: Strong: escalates deliberately — documentation, a named process, involving the next rank — and says so without threatening. Weak: repeats the first conversation louder.
items.teaching_focus: Progressive response, which is where the rank actually lives.

items.text: PROBE 8 — What did YOU do wrong here?
items.answer: Strong: something concrete — the assignment was loose, the PAR interval was too long, expectations were never stated. Weak: 'nothing, but I'll be more vigilant.'
items.teaching_focus: The question that separates a candidate from an officer.

items.text: PROBE 9 — What have you changed since?
items.answer: Strong: one specific, checkable change already made. Weak: intentions in the future tense.
items.teaching_focus: Past tense beats future tense on every board.

items.text: PROBE 10 — If I asked him about this conversation, what would he say?
items.answer: Strong: confident about what was said and how it landed, and honest if it landed badly. Weak: has no idea, which reveals the conversation was a formality.
items.teaching_focus: The closing probe that tests whether anything real happened.

components.label: Panel rubric
components.instructions: One per candidate. Score during the rep. Share the completed sheet in the debrief — a filled rubric is a conversation, an impression is an argument.

items.text: Our board's format — fill first
fields: Our accountability and PAR procedure reference

items.text: Score
fields: Owned it at probe 3 without qualifying (Y/N)
Named anyone else as the cause (Y/N — this is a negative)
Specific words of the conversation given (Y/N)

items.text: Delivery
fields: Eye contact held under probe 3 and probe 8
Did the answer get shorter or longer as pressure rose
One thing to fix before the next rep
items.teaching_focus: Answers that lengthen under pressure are a candidate talking themselves into trouble.

components.label: Solo self-review sheet
components.instructions: Film yourself, not just audio — a board reads posture, hands and eye contact and none of that survives a voice recording. Answer the probes cold from the printed cards, then score your own film against the rubric.

items.text: Setup
fields: Camera at seated eye level, framing head and hands
items.teaching_focus: No restarts. A fumbled answer is a rep.

items.text: On playback
fields: Where my hands did something distracting
The probe where I ran out of substance
The one probe I will re-run three times today

sources: Department accountability procedure and promotional process format (user-supplied)

packs.title: Crew Conflict Board Kit — 10 Probes and a Panel Rubric
packs.summary: A two-member conflict brief, ten probes that escalate from the facts into the candidate's own contribution and their duty to the rest of the crew, and the rubric. The probes are built to punish the two easy answers: separate them, or wait and see.
packs.removes_prep: The drill needs board question cards and supplies none. Interpersonal scenarios are the ones candidates prepare least and boards weight most, and the difficulty is entirely in the follow-ups — a candidate rehearsing alone asks themselves only comfortable questions.
packs.local_fill_note: Your department's conduct, grievance and harassment procedures decide where a conflict stops being yours to manage and becomes a formal matter. Write those thresholds on the rubric — a candidate who cannot name them will get probe 9 wrong.

components.label: Candidate brief and escalating probes
components.instructions: Brief read once, then the clock. Probes in order. The panel does not react to the candidate's answers; a real board is uncomfortably neutral and the rehearsal must be too.

items.text: BRIEF — You are a lieutenant. Two of your firefighters, both competent, have stopped speaking to each other except when the job requires it. It has been going on for three weeks. Last shift, on a working fire, one of them hesitated before taking a tool from the other. Nobody has complained to you.
items.teaching_focus: Nobody complained. The candidate has to justify acting at all.

items.text: PROBE 1 — What is the actual problem here?
items.answer: Strong: names it as an operational safety problem, not a personality problem, and points at the hesitation on the fireground. Weak: 'they need to get along.'
items.teaching_focus: Framing it as a job problem is what gives the officer standing to act.

items.text: PROBE 2 — Nobody has complained. Why is this yours to deal with?
items.answer: Strong: because crew function is the officer's responsibility whether or not anyone asks. Weak: hesitates, or says they would wait for a complaint.
items.teaching_focus: Acting without being asked. This probe eliminates a lot of candidates.

items.text: PROBE 3 — What do you do first, specifically?
items.answer: Strong: talks to each one separately, first, and listens before deciding anything. Weak: puts them in a room together immediately, which is the most common wrong answer.
items.teaching_focus: Separate conversations first. Joint conversations without information become a fight with a witness.

items.text: PROBE 4 — One says the other has been talking about him behind his back. The other says nothing is wrong. Now what?
items.answer: Strong: does not adjudicate the truth; addresses the observable behavior and the operational standard. Weak: tries to establish who is lying.
items.teaching_focus: You cannot investigate feelings. You can require conduct.

items.text: PROBE 5 — What exactly do you require of them? Give me the words.
items.answer: Strong: a concrete, observable standard — direct professional communication on the job, every time, starting now — with a stated consequence. Weak: 'be professional', which is unmeasurable.
items.teaching_focus: A standard that can be observed and therefore enforced.

items.text: PROBE 6 — What is your responsibility to the other three people on the crew?
items.answer: Strong: they have been working around this for three weeks and they need to see it addressed; says what they will and will not be told. Weak: has not considered them.
items.teaching_focus: The rest of the crew, again. The most reliable differentiator on interpersonal questions.

items.text: PROBE 7 — What was your part in this going on for three weeks?
items.answer: Strong: names it — did not notice, or noticed and hoped, or was avoiding a difficult conversation. Weak: 'I only just found out', when the hesitation happened in front of them.
items.teaching_focus: The ownership probe. Boards ask it on every interpersonal scenario.

items.text: PROBE 8 — One of them is significantly senior to you and was passed over for your job. Does your answer change?
items.answer: Strong: the standard does not change; the approach acknowledges the situation honestly and privately. Weak: either backs down or over-asserts rank.
items.teaching_focus: The complication that is true in half of all real promotions.

items.text: PROBE 9 — During your conversation, one of them alleges the other made a discriminatory remark. What do you do?
items.answer: Strong: stops managing it informally and follows the department's formal procedure, by name, immediately, and says so. Weak: keeps trying to mediate.
items.teaching_focus: Knowing the exact point at which informal management becomes misconduct on the officer's part.

items.text: PROBE 10 — Six weeks later they are civil but cold. Is that success?
items.answer: Strong: yes, if the operational standard is met — friendship is not the objective, and says so without cynicism. Weak: sets an unachievable target and commits to more intervention.
items.teaching_focus: Knowing what good enough looks like.

components.label: Panel rubric
components.instructions: Score live. The negative rows matter as much as the positive ones — boards remember the wrong move longer than the right one.

items.text: Our thresholds — fill first
fields: Our conduct procedure and when it applies
What we must document and where

items.text: Score
fields: Gave an observable standard in actual words (Y/N)
Addressed the rest of the crew (Y/N)

items.text: Delivery
fields: Longest pause, and at which probe
Did they ask the panel for information they should have assumed

sources: Department conduct, grievance and harassment procedures (user-supplied and authoritative)

packs.title: Exam Question Deck Builder — 40 Stems and a Blueprint
packs.summary: Forty question stems across supervision, policy judgment, tactics, and fire behavior with the correct-reasoning note but no keyed answer — the answer comes from your department's own policy — plus a blueprint sheet for weighting your deck to your announced exam and a distractor-writing guide.
packs.removes_prep: The drill is literally 'Build Your Own Lieutenant Exam Question Deck', and building one is a week of evenings. Worse, candidates write questions about what they already know, so a self-built deck systematically omits the candidate's weak areas — which is what the deck was for.
packs.local_fill_note: NO ANSWER IS KEYED, on purpose. On a promotional exam the correct answer is the one your department's policy, SOPs and adopted references support, and those differ everywhere. Each stem carries a reasoning note; you supply the answer and cite where you found it. A stem you cannot source is a study gap, not a bad question.

components.label: Deck blueprint
components.instructions: Fill this from your announced exam notice BEFORE writing a single card. A deck weighted differently from the exam trains the wrong proportions, which is the most common self-study error.

items.text: From the exam announcement
fields: Announced subject areas and their weightings
Number of questions and time allowed
Question format — single best answer, multiple response, scenario sets

items.text: My deck weighting
fields: Cards on fire behavior and building construction
Does this match the announced weighting (Y/N)
items.teaching_focus: Count and compare. Candidates over-weight tactics and under-weight administration every time.

items.text: My weak areas — be honest
fields: Subject I would rather not study
Last score or self-assessment in it
Who can check my answers in that area
items.teaching_focus: The deck should be lopsided toward what you are bad at, not balanced.

components.label: Forty question stems
components.instructions: Write each stem on a card. On the back, write the answer YOUR policy supports, the citation, and one sentence on why the near-miss alternative is wrong. Then drill the deck timed. A card without a citation is not finished.

items.text: A member's assignment is complete and they begin another task on their own initiative. Under your accountability policy, what is required of the officer?
items.teaching_focus: Accountability policy applied to an ordinary event.

items.text: Two members are assigned to a task requiring three. What is the officer's obligation before beginning?
items.teaching_focus: Refusing or modifying an assignment, with policy behind it.

items.text: A member reports an injury at the end of a shift that they say happened earlier. What does your policy require and in what order?
items.teaching_focus: Reporting timelines, which are almost always on the exam.

items.text: You suspect a member is impaired at work. State your immediate obligations.
items.teaching_focus: The scenario with the least room for improvisation.

items.text: A probationary member's performance is below standard at the midpoint of probation. What must be documented and when?
items.teaching_focus: Probationary process, which candidates rarely read.

items.text: A member refuses an order they believe is unsafe. State how you proceed.
items.teaching_focus: Both halves: the member's right and the officer's obligation.

items.text: Under your policy, at what point does an accountability report become a mayday?
items.teaching_focus: The definitional question. Ties to RIT-006.

items.text: State the required elements of your initial radio report.
items.teaching_focus: Rote recall the exam will test verbatim.

items.text: Your department's two-in/two-out requirement: state it, and state the exception.
items.teaching_focus: Regulatory recall with a named exception.

items.text: Who may declare a change from offensive to defensive operations, and what must be done immediately after?
items.teaching_focus: Authority plus the follow-through step.

items.text: State the required interval for a PAR under your policy and the events that trigger one out of interval.
items.teaching_focus: Interval plus triggers. Candidates learn the interval only.

items.text: A rapid intervention crew is required at what point in an incident, per your policy?
items.teaching_focus: Timing, not existence.

items.text: State your policy's air-management decision points.
items.teaching_focus: The RIT-008 numbers, examined.

items.text: What is required before a member enters an IDLH atmosphere?
items.teaching_focus: A regulatory list the exam will expect complete.

items.text: State the elements of your incident action plan, in order.
items.teaching_focus: Structure recall.

items.text: You arrive at a working fire and a chief officer is already on scene but has not announced command. What do you do?
items.teaching_focus: Command establishment, ambiguous case.

items.text: Describe when your department requires a formal transfer of command versus an informal one.
items.teaching_focus: Ties to OFF-005.

items.text: State the factors in a risk-benefit analysis as your department defines them.
items.teaching_focus: Definitions the candidate must use the department's words for.

items.text: A vacant structure with a working fire and no reported occupants. State the strategic decision and the policy basis.
items.teaching_focus: Applying a risk framework to the classic case.

items.text: What conditions require establishment of a collapse zone, and how is it dimensioned per your policy?
items.teaching_focus: A number the exam loves.

items.text: Describe the difference between a hazard and a risk as your adopted reference defines them.
items.teaching_focus: Terminology precision.

items.text: State the stages of fire development and the transition your adopted reference identifies as most dangerous to crews.
items.teaching_focus: Fire behavior recall.

items.text: Explain flow path in one paragraph as you would to a probationary firefighter.
items.teaching_focus: Explaining, which some boards score directly.

items.text: Describe the indicators of imminent flashover.
items.teaching_focus: Recall with an application question hiding in it.

items.text: Identify the five types of building construction and the primary collapse concern of each.
items.teaching_focus: A near-certain exam item.

items.text: Describe how lightweight truss construction changes your operational time frame.
items.teaching_focus: Ties to LODD-005.

items.text: State the friction loss in your department's standard attack line at its target flow, and show the calculation.
items.teaching_focus: The DRV-006 numbers, examined.

items.text: Calculate the pump discharge pressure for a described layout.
items.teaching_focus: A worked calculation with your own coefficients.

items.text: State the required fire flow for a described structure using your department's adopted method.
items.teaching_focus: Method-dependent, so the citation matters more than the number.

items.text: Describe your department's water supply options for an area without hydrants.
items.teaching_focus: Local operational knowledge.

items.text: State the standpipe outlet pressure your policy specifies and why it may differ from a nozzle's rated pressure.
items.teaching_focus: Ties to MCO-004.

items.text: Describe the difference between ventilation-limited and fuel-limited fire behavior and what each implies tactically.
items.teaching_focus: The concept most likely to appear as a scenario stem.

items.text: A member is due for an annual evaluation and has one documented performance issue. Describe your approach.
items.teaching_focus: Evaluation process plus judgment.

items.text: Describe your obligations when a member raises a safety concern about a departmental practice.
items.teaching_focus: Upward communication, rarely studied.

items.text: State what must be documented after an incident involving a firefighter injury.
items.teaching_focus: Documentation recall.

items.text: Describe the purpose and required content of a post-incident analysis under your policy.
items.teaching_focus: Administrative process.

items.text: You are ordered to do something you believe conflicts with policy. Describe your response.
items.teaching_focus: Professional obligation under conflict.

items.text: Describe your role in your department's respiratory protection program as a company officer.
items.teaching_focus: A program candidates assume is someone else's job.

items.text: State the training records you are responsible for and their retention requirement.
items.teaching_focus: Records, dull and reliably examined.

items.text: THE CARD YOU WRITE — the subject you avoided while building this deck. Write three stems on it.
items.teaching_focus: The whole blueprint exercise, enforced by one card.

components.label: Distractor-writing guide
components.instructions: Read before writing your own answer options. A question with obviously wrong alternatives trains nothing, and writing plausible wrong answers is the skill that makes a self-built deck worth drilling.

items.text: Write FOUR options where three are plausible to someone who half-knows the material. If you can eliminate two by common sense, the card is worthless.
items.teaching_focus: The core rule.

items.text: Best distractor: correct in a different jurisdiction or a superseded edition. This is how real exams punish stale study.
items.teaching_focus: The distractor type most likely to catch you on the real exam.

items.text: Second best: correct action, wrong order. Tests sequence rather than recognition.
items.teaching_focus: Order questions are common and candidates under-prepare them.

items.text: Third: correct for a different rank. Tests whether the candidate knows the boundary of their authority.
items.teaching_focus: A distractor that teaches the rank as well as the fact.

items.text: Avoid: absolutes, 'all of the above', and anything longer than the other options. Real exams avoid them and so should your practice.
items.teaching_focus: Not training yourself on tells that will not be there.

items.text: Cite everything. A card whose answer you cannot source is a study gap you have just written down — keep it and go find the source.
items.teaching_focus: The citation discipline that turns deck-building into studying.

sources: Self-authored stems, blueprint and distractor guide
Department policy, SOPs and the exam announcement's adopted references (user-supplied; no answers keyed here)

packs.title: Solo Timed Set Kit — Session Structure and Stem-Reading Card
packs.summary: Four timed set structures at increasing pressure, a stem-reading card covering the specific ways a well-written question misleads, and the error log that sorts every wrong answer into knowledge, reading, or timing — because those three failures have completely different fixes.
packs.removes_prep: The drill needs a question deck and a timed structure and supplies neither. The deck comes from OFF-009; what this pack adds is the part that makes solo drilling work — a fixed structure and an error taxonomy, because a candidate marking their own paper without one just knows they got twelve wrong.
packs.local_fill_note: Set the per-question time from your announced exam: total time divided by question count, minus a review margin you choose. Drilling at a comfortable pace trains a pace you will not have.

components.label: Four session structures
components.instructions: Work up the ladder over several weeks. Do not skip to session 4 — the point is that pressure is added one variable at a time so you can tell which one breaks you.

items.text: SESSION 1 — Untimed accuracy
items.teaching_focus: Establishes whether the problem is knowledge at all. If accuracy is poor untimed, timing is not your issue.

items.text: SESSION 2 — At exam pace
items.teaching_focus: The gap between session 1 and 2 accuracy is your timing cost, as a number.

items.text: SESSION 3 — At pace, after physical work
fields: Work done first — stairs, PPE circuit, whatever
Where in the set the errors clustered
items.teaching_focus: Some promotional processes run written and physical on the same day. Errors cluster late; find out where.

items.text: SESSION 4 — At pace, with an interruption
fields: Interruption used — a phone alarm, someone entering, a deliberate distraction
Questions missed in the two minutes after it
items.teaching_focus: Recovery time is trainable and nobody trains it.

components.label: Stem-reading card
components.instructions: Read before every timed set until it is automatic. Every line is a way a well-written question is misread by someone who knows the material.

items.text: Find the actual question first. Read the last sentence of the stem before the scenario. Half of a long stem is often context you do not need.
items.teaching_focus: Saves time and prevents answering a question that was not asked.

items.text: Circle the qualifier: FIRST, BEST, MOST, LEAST, EXCEPT, NOT. More than one option is usually correct; the qualifier picks between them.
items.teaching_focus: The single largest source of wrong answers among candidates who know the material.

items.text: Note the rank the question puts you in. An answer correct for a chief is wrong for a lieutenant, and exams exploit this deliberately.
items.teaching_focus: Matches the distractor type in OFF-009's guide.

items.text: Watch for the sequence question in disguise: 'what do you do first' is not 'what do you do'.
items.teaching_focus: Order questions look like knowledge questions.

items.text: Answer from policy, not from experience. What your crew actually does and what your policy requires may differ, and the exam scores the policy.
items.teaching_focus: The hardest habit for an experienced candidate to break.

items.text: Flag and move. A question you have read twice without progress will not yield on the third read while the clock runs. Mark it and come back.
items.teaching_focus: Time management as a decision, not a drift.

items.text: Change an answer only for a reason you can state in words. 'It feels wrong' is not one.
items.teaching_focus: Second-guessing costs more marks than it saves.

components.label: Error log
components.instructions: Every wrong answer gets a row and a category. The categories are the point: three failures with three different fixes, and treating them all as 'study more' is why solo preparation plateaus.

items.text: Error row
fields: If reading: which qualifier did I miss
If timing: how far into the set was it

items.text: Category totals after each session
items.teaching_focus: Knowledge → study. Reading → the stem card. Timing → pace drills. Wrong diagnosis wastes weeks.

items.text: Action from this session
fields: The single subject to study next
My pace versus my target pace

sources: Self-authored session structures, stem card and error log
Exam announcement pacing and adopted references (user-supplied)

packs.title: Blind-Draw Size-Up Cards — 16 First-Due Scenarios
packs.summary: Sixteen first-due scenario cards written to be drawn cold, each stating what you see on arrival and nothing else, with the elements a complete size-up must contain on the back and a scoring strip. Deliberately weighted toward the buildings candidates have not prepared for.
packs.removes_prep: The drill needs blind-draw scenario cards, a worksheet and a report format, and supplies none. A candidate writing their own cards knows what is on them, which destroys the blind draw — the one thing the drill depends on.
packs.local_fill_note: Substitute your own district's building types and your department's report format. A scenario in somebody else's district trains a generic answer, and boards can tell.

components.label: Sixteen arrival scenarios
components.instructions: Shuffle face down. Draw one, read it once, then 60 seconds to a full size-up out loud on the recorder — building, conditions, actions, needs, mode. No restarts. Check the back afterwards.

items.text: Two-story wood-frame dwelling, smoke showing from a second-floor window, mid-afternoon, car in the driveway.
items.answer: Must include: construction and height, the location and character of the smoke, a mode, a first assignment, and a search decision reasoned from the car. Watch for: no mode declared.
items.teaching_focus: Baseline. Everyone should pass this.

items.text: Same dwelling, 0300, no vehicles, no smoke showing, a neighbor reports an alarm sounding inside.
items.answer: Must include: an investigation mode stated as such, and a plan for entry and for what would escalate it. Watch for: candidates who cannot commit to anything because nothing is showing.
items.teaching_focus: Sizing up an absence of evidence.

items.text: Single-story ranch, heavy smoke from the eaves on all sides, nothing visible at windows.
items.answer: Must include: recognition of a possible attic or void fire, construction concern, and a decision about the roof. Watch for: treating it as a room-and-contents fire.
items.teaching_focus: Smoke location as the whole story.

items.text: Three-story garden apartment, fire showing from a second-floor unit, occupants in the parking lot, one reported missing.
items.answer: Must include: unit identification, exposure units above and beside, a search assignment tied to the report, and accountability in a repeating layout.
items.teaching_focus: Exposures inside the same building.

items.text: Commercial strip unit, light smoke, security bars, 0200, no occupants expected.
items.answer: Must include: access problem named, rear unconfirmed, and a mode that reflects the risk-benefit of an unoccupied building.
items.teaching_focus: Justifying a slower approach out loud.

items.text: Large single-story big-box commercial, light smoke from the rear roof area, business closed.
items.answer: Must include: building size and its stretch implication, open-span construction, and a stated need for resources beyond the first alarm.
items.teaching_focus: Asking for help in the initial report.

items.text: Two-story mixed-use main street, fire in the ground-floor commercial, apartments above, evening.
items.answer: Must include: life hazard above the fire as the priority, stair access, and an exposure assessment on both sides.
items.teaching_focus: Occupancy stacking.

items.text: Dwelling with a walk-out basement on a downslope, smoke from the lower level at the rear, nothing from the street.
items.answer: Must include: recognition that the building is below grade at the rear, and a size-up that could only be made by going round. Watch for: candidates who never mention the 360.
items.teaching_focus: The building that is different from the back.

items.text: Detached garage well involved, attached to nothing, but three feet from the dwelling.
items.answer: Must include: the exposure as the priority and a stated decision about the dwelling.
items.teaching_focus: The fire is not the problem.

items.text: Vehicle fire in an underground parking structure.
items.answer: Must include: below grade, confined space and ventilation problems, standpipe or supply arrangement, and a very different resource picture from a street car fire.
items.teaching_focus: A routine fire in a hostile place.

items.text: Six-story residential, smoke in a stairwell, no fire located, alarm sounding, occupants self-evacuating past you.
items.answer: Must include: stair selection for attack and for evacuation, locating the fire before committing, and a lobby-control function.
items.teaching_focus: Ties to MCO-004.

items.text: Working fire in a dwelling, and on arrival a bystander tells you two children are inside and points at a window.
items.answer: Must include: a mode, a rescue assignment, a line to protect it, and an explicit statement of what is being accepted. Watch for: a candidate who abandons structure entirely under emotional pressure.
items.teaching_focus: Keeping the format under the worst possible information.

items.text: Nothing showing at a reported structure fire, occupant on the lawn saying they put it out.
items.answer: Must include: not accepting the claim, an investigation with a thermal imager and an opened-up check, and a stated hold on releasing companies.
items.teaching_focus: The call that goes wrong after everyone relaxes.

items.text: Barn or agricultural structure, fully involved, no exposures, well water only, twenty minutes from a hydrant.
items.answer: Must include: defensive, water supply as the dominant problem, tanker or shuttle request in the initial report.
items.teaching_focus: Rural water supply, which urban-trained candidates fumble.

items.text: Working fire, and while you are transmitting your initial report a second company arrives and begins operating without direction.
items.answer: Must include: finishing the report, then command and assignment of the freelancing company. Watch for: abandoning the report.
items.teaching_focus: Two things at once, in an initial report.

items.text: THE CARD YOU WRITE — the worst building in your first-due. Write the arrival on a blank card and shuffle it in.
fields: What you would see on arrival at 0300
The complication that makes it your worst
What you would need in the initial report
items.teaching_focus: The one card that is definitely on your real exam, because it is definitely on your real fireground.

components.label: Scoring strip
components.instructions: One per card, marked from the recording with the card visible. Under 60 seconds, every element present, and a mode declared — the same standard as OFF-001, applied to a candidate rather than an officer.

items.text: Format
fields: Building: size, height, occupancy, construction — all four (Y/N)
Conditions: location and character of smoke or fire (Y/N)
items.teaching_focus: Mode declared is the row that fails most often and matters most.

items.text: Candidate quality
fields: Did they ask for information the card did not give (Y/N)
Did they invent facts not on the card (Y/N — negative)
items.teaching_focus: Inventing facts is the tell of a candidate who cannot work with incomplete information.

items.text: Across a session
fields: The element I most often drop
The building type I am worst on

sources: Department report format SOP and local building stock (user-supplied)

packs.title: Escalating Incident Board — 5 Escalations and Checkpoint Cards
packs.summary: Five incidents that escalate in stages with the injects timed, checkpoint cards that force a decision at each stage, and the decision-log worksheet. Built so the candidate has to revise a plan they already committed to — which is the thing assessment centers actually test.
packs.removes_prep: The drill needs escalation cards and a worksheet and supplies none. Writing an escalation that stays coherent across five stages is genuinely hard: each inject has to invalidate part of the previous plan without contradicting the facts already given.
packs.local_fill_note: Set resources and response times to your own department's. An escalation that arrives faster than your mutual aid ever could trains a plan you cannot execute.

components.label: Five escalations
components.instructions: Give stage 1 and require a committed plan on the board before stage 2 is read. Injects come on the clock whether or not the candidate is ready — that is the point. Never let them redo an earlier stage.

items.text: ESCALATION A — Residential. Stage 1: room-and-contents fire, one line, primary underway. Stage 2 (+3 min): the fire has extended to the attic. Stage 3 (+6 min): a member reports the ceiling is coming down. Stage 4 (+8 min): PAR reveals one company unaccounted for. Stage 5 (+10 min): the missing company reports in from outside — they exited a different way and did not announce it.
items.answer: Tests: extension recognized and a second line committed; withdrawal considered at stage 3; mayday process at stage 4; and — the real test — whether the candidate treats stage 5 as relief or as an accountability failure to be addressed.
items.teaching_focus: Stage 5 is the assessment. Most candidates exhale and move on.

items.text: ESCALATION B — Commercial. Stage 1: light smoke, investigating. Stage 2 (+3): fire found in a concealed space. Stage 3 (+5): it has run the length of the void. Stage 4 (+7): the roof is sagging over the involved section. Stage 5 (+9): a crew is still on the roof.
items.answer: Tests: escalation from investigation to offensive; void fire recognized as a whole-building problem; defensive decision at stage 4; and whether the roof crew was ever tracked. The candidate who ordered them up at stage 2 and forgot them fails stage 5.
items.teaching_focus: Accounting for the assignment you gave four minutes ago.

items.text: ESCALATION C — Apartment. Stage 1: fire in one unit, occupants evacuating. Stage 2 (+2): a report of a person in the unit above. Stage 3 (+4): the reporting party is now unsure. Stage 4 (+6): the fire has extended to the unit above. Stage 5 (+8): a second report, a different unit, also unconfirmed.
items.answer: Tests: acting on unconfirmed reports, revising when the information degrades at stage 3, and — at stage 5 — whether the candidate can decline to chase a third search with the resources present, and say why.
items.teaching_focus: Managing information that gets worse rather than better.

items.text: ESCALATION D — Water supply. Stage 1: working fire, tank water, supply being established. Stage 2 (+2): the hydrant is dry. Stage 3 (+4): tank water is nearly gone with crews inside. Stage 4 (+6): the next hydrant is 800 ft away. Stage 5 (+8): mutual aid tanker is 15 minutes out.
items.answer: Tests: whether crews are withdrawn at stage 3 before the water stops rather than after, and whether the stage 5 plan is defensive rather than optimistic.
items.teaching_focus: Deciding before the resource runs out. Candidates consistently decide one stage too late.

items.text: ESCALATION E — Everything. Stage 1: working fire, adequate resources. Stage 2 (+2): a member falls and is injured, not trapped. Stage 3 (+4): weather deteriorates sharply. Stage 4 (+6): a second incident is dispatched in your district and takes your remaining company. Stage 5 (+8): the injured member's condition is worse than first reported.
items.answer: Tests: managing an injury without stopping the incident, external resource loss, and whether the candidate ever considered that the whole operation may no longer be supportable. The strong answer at stage 5 is often to go defensive and free people.
items.teaching_focus: Knowing when the incident has outgrown the resources and saying so.

components.label: Checkpoint cards
components.instructions: Hand the candidate the matching checkpoint card at each stage. Four questions, answered aloud, before the next inject. They are identical every stage on purpose — the discipline is the repetition.

items.text: CHECKPOINT — answer all four, out loud, now.
fields: 1. What has changed since my last plan
2. What in my plan is now wrong
3. Who is where, and when did I last confirm it
4. What is my trigger to go defensive
items.teaching_focus: Question 2 is the one candidates skip. A plan is revised by finding what is wrong with it, not by adding to it.

items.text: Why the same four every time
items.answer: Because an assessment center is measuring whether you have a repeatable method under escalating pressure, not whether you can improvise five different clever responses. A candidate who visibly runs the same check at every stage reads as an officer.
items.teaching_focus: Visible method is itself a scored behavior.

components.label: Decision log
components.instructions: The candidate keeps this on the board as they go. Assessors score the log as much as the talking, and a candidate who cannot maintain it under escalation is showing you something real.

items.text: Stage row
items.teaching_focus: 'What I explicitly kept' — deciding not to change something is a decision and should be visible.

items.text: After the last stage
fields: Which stage I was slowest on
A decision I made one stage too late
A plan element I never revisited
Whether my defensive trigger ever changed

sources: Self-authored escalations, checkpoint cards and decision log

packs.title: Coaching Conversation Kit — 6 Cases, Script Frame, Rubric
packs.summary: Six underperformance cases that each fail a different way, a conversation script frame built on observable behavior rather than character, and the rubric — plus the role-player card that tells the other person exactly how to be difficult, which is what makes the rehearsal worth anything.
packs.removes_prep: The drill needs scenario cards and supplies none. The harder gap is the other side of the conversation: a candidate rehearsing alone gets a cooperative imaginary firefighter, and the whole difficulty of coaching is that the real one is defensive.
packs.local_fill_note: Your department's performance management, documentation and progressive discipline procedures decide when a coaching conversation must become a formal one. Write those thresholds on the rubric — case 6 cannot be answered without them.

components.label: Six cases
components.instructions: One case per session. The candidate gets the case; the role-player gets the case plus their own card. Run it as a real conversation, timed, filmed. Do not stop it when it goes badly — the recovery is the skill.

items.text: CASE 1 — SKILL. A competent firefighter of eight years is consistently slow on SCBA donning, well outside the standard, and has been for months. Nobody has said anything.
items.answer: Tests: raising a skill deficit with an experienced member without humiliating them. Strong answers separate the person's competence from the specific skill, give the number, and offer reps rather than criticism.
items.teaching_focus: The number does the work. 'You're slow' is an opinion; a time against a standard is a fact.

items.text: CASE 2 — WILL. A capable firefighter does the minimum. Nothing is wrong, nothing is good. Training days are endured.
items.answer: Tests: addressing effort, which has no measurable standard. Strong answers find something specific and observable rather than talking about attitude, and ask a genuine question about what changed.
items.teaching_focus: The hardest case, because there is no metric and no incident to point at.

items.text: CASE 3 — SAFETY. A firefighter has twice been seen without their hood properly deployed on an interior attack.
items.answer: Tests: whether the candidate treats this as a coaching matter or a correction. Strong answers correct it immediately and unambiguously, then coach — and state the consequence of a third time.
items.teaching_focus: Some things are corrected first and coached second. Knowing which is the officer's judgment.

items.text: CASE 4 — PERSONAL. A normally strong firefighter's performance has fallen off sharply over six weeks. You have heard second-hand that something is happening at home.
items.answer: Tests: addressing performance without becoming a counselor or ignoring the human situation. Strong answers stay on the observable change, offer the department's support resources by name, and do not require disclosure.
items.teaching_focus: Naming the support resources. A candidate who cannot name them has not prepared.

items.text: CASE 5 — SENIOR. A firefighter with twenty years, widely respected, is dismissive of new tactics and says so in front of probationary members.
items.answer: Tests: rank versus standing. Strong answers address the effect on the probationers as the concrete harm, private and direct, and use the member's influence rather than fighting it.
items.teaching_focus: The harm is downstream, and that is what gives the officer standing.

items.text: CASE 6 — REPEAT. This is the third documented conversation on the same issue and nothing has changed.
items.answer: Tests: knowing when coaching is finished. Strong answers move to the formal process by name, document, involve the next rank, and say plainly that this is no longer a coaching conversation.
items.teaching_focus: Coaching forever is a failure of nerve dressed as patience.

components.label: Role-player card — how to be difficult
components.instructions: For the other person only. Pick ONE resistance per rep so the candidate faces one problem at a time. Do not be impossible; be realistic, and yield if the candidate genuinely does the work.

items.text: RESISTANCE A — Deflect to someone else. 'Half the crew does that.' Hold it twice, then yield if they bring it back to you specifically.
items.teaching_focus: Tests whether the candidate can decline to discuss third parties.

items.text: RESISTANCE B — Minimize. 'It's not a big deal.' Ask them to explain why it matters. Yield only to a concrete consequence, not to a rule citation.
items.teaching_focus: Forces the candidate to explain the WHY rather than assert authority.

items.text: RESISTANCE C — Go silent. Answer in as few words as possible. Do not help. Yield slightly if they tolerate the silence rather than filling it.
items.teaching_focus: Most candidates cannot sit in a silence and talk themselves into a worse position.

items.text: RESISTANCE D — Get emotional. Not aggressive — upset. Yield if they acknowledge it without abandoning the point or rescuing you.
items.teaching_focus: Staying on the point while being humane. The most common real difficulty.

items.text: RESISTANCE E — Attack the officer. 'You've only had the job five minutes.' Yield if they neither escalate nor apologize for their rank.
items.teaching_focus: The one that rattles new officers most.

items.text: RESISTANCE F — Agree with everything, mean none of it. Enthusiastic compliance, no specifics. Yield only if they pin down a specific action and a follow-up date.
items.teaching_focus: Fake agreement ends more coaching conversations than conflict does.

components.label: Script frame and rubric
components.instructions: The frame is a structure, not a script to read. Fill your department's thresholds first. Score from the film.

items.text: OUR THRESHOLDS — fill first
fields: When a conversation must be documented
When it becomes formal performance management
Our member support resources, by name

items.text: Frame
fields: OPEN — the specific observable behavior, with a time and place
IMPACT — the concrete consequence, on the job or the crew
ASK — a real question, and then silence
CLOSE — the specific action, and the follow-up date
items.teaching_focus: ASK before STANDARD. Candidates who deliver the standard first get compliance and no change.

items.text: Rubric
fields: Opened with observable behavior, not character (Y/N)
Asked a genuine question and waited (Y/N)
Talked about attitude or personality (Y/N — negative)
Resistance handled without escalating or collapsing (Y/N)

items.text: From the film
fields: Ratio of my talking to theirs
One fix for the next rep
items.teaching_focus: If the officer did most of the talking, it was a lecture.

sources: Self-authored cases, role-player card, frame and rubric
Department performance management, documentation, progressive discipline and member support procedures (user-supplied and authoritative)

packs.title: Unsafe Act & Trust Repair Kit — 6 Cases and a Two-Part Rubric
packs.summary: Six unsafe-act cases with the immediate correction and the trust repair scored as two separate conversations, because candidates who handle the first well routinely never have the second — plus the role-player card and a crew-level repair sheet.
packs.removes_prep: The drill needs scenario cards and supplies none, and it has a structural difficulty no candidate solves alone: it is two conversations days apart, and rehearsing only the confrontation trains exactly half the skill the drill is named for.
packs.local_fill_note: Your department's immediate-danger stop-work authority, its reporting requirements after an unsafe act, and its discipline thresholds all govern. Write them on the rubric before the first case — case 1 turns on whether the candidate knows their stop-work authority.

components.label: Six cases
components.instructions: Run each case as TWO reps on the same day: the correction, then a short break, then the repair conversation set some days later. Score them separately. A candidate who nails the first and fumbles the second has found the point of the drill.

items.text: CASE 1 — IN THE MOMENT. On the fireground, a member starts to enter without their facepiece sealed. You are ten feet away and there is a working fire.
items.answer: Correction: immediate, physical if necessary, unambiguous, no discussion. Repair: later, privately, explaining why it was immediate and hearing what happened. Tests whether the candidate knows they can stop work and does it without hesitating.
items.teaching_focus: Correction is not a conversation. The conversation comes after.

items.text: CASE 2 — WITNESSED BY THE CREW. A member takes a shortcut on a ladder placement in front of the whole company and it worked out fine.
items.answer: Correction: in front of the crew, because they all saw it and silence is endorsement — but short and about the act. Repair: privately, because a public correction costs the member something that has to be given back.
items.teaching_focus: Public act, public correction, private repair. Candidates get this order wrong in both directions.

items.text: CASE 3 — YOUR OWN ORDER CAUSED IT. A member did something unsafe because your assignment was ambiguous.
items.answer: Correction: stop the act. Repair: own the ambiguity out loud, to the member and to the crew. Tests whether the candidate can correct and apologize in the same episode without undermining either.
items.teaching_focus: The hardest combination in the pack, and the one that builds the most trust.

items.text: CASE 4 — SENIOR MEMBER, MINOR ACT. A twenty-year firefighter cuts a corner you would correct in a probationary member.
items.answer: Correction: the same standard, delivered with awareness of the audience. Repair: acknowledging their experience without conceding the standard. Tests consistency under social pressure.
items.teaching_focus: A standard that bends by seniority is not a standard, and the crew is watching to see if it does.

items.text: CASE 5 — IT WENT WRONG. The unsafe act resulted in a minor injury.
items.answer: Correction is moot; the work now is care, reporting, and investigation. Repair is harder because the member is embarrassed and possibly frightened. Tests whether the candidate can separate the reporting obligation from blame.
items.teaching_focus: Reporting and blame are different processes, and conflating them stops future reporting.

items.text: CASE 6 — REPEAT AFTER REPAIR. You corrected it, you repaired it well, and three weeks later they did it again.
items.answer: The repair worked and the behavior did not change, which means this is now a discipline matter and not a trust matter. Tests whether the candidate can escalate without treating the earlier repair as a failure or a betrayal.
items.teaching_focus: Escalating after a good relationship is harder than escalating after a bad one.

components.label: Role-player card
components.instructions: One resistance per rep, and a DIFFERENT posture for the repair conversation than for the correction — that shift is what the candidate has to adapt to.

items.text: In the CORRECTION: comply immediately but visibly resent it. Say nothing. The candidate must not mistake compliance for resolution.
items.teaching_focus: Silence at the correction is why the repair conversation exists.

items.text: In the CORRECTION: argue briefly — 'I had it under control.' Stop when told to. Tests whether the candidate debates on the fireground.
items.teaching_focus: The fireground is not a place for a discussion, and saying so is a skill.

items.text: In the REPAIR: be cold and formal. Yield only if they name the awkwardness out loud.
items.teaching_focus: Naming the awkwardness is what unsticks it.

items.text: In the REPAIR: be over-apologetic and self-critical. Yield if they neither pile on nor reassure you out of the standard.
items.teaching_focus: Managing someone who is punishing themselves harder than you would.

items.text: In the REPAIR: raise a grievance about how it was done in front of the crew. Yield if they acknowledge the cost without withdrawing the correction.
items.teaching_focus: Both things true at once: right to correct, and it cost them something.

items.text: In the REPAIR: tell them the crew thinks they overreacted. Yield if they check it rather than accept or dismiss it.
items.teaching_focus: Testing whether the candidate seeks information or defends.

components.label: Two-part rubric and crew repair sheet
components.instructions: Two scores per case, never one. Then the crew sheet, because an unsafe act witnessed by five people is five relationships, not one.

items.text: OUR RULES — fill first
fields: Our stop-work authority — who has it and in what words
Reporting required after an unsafe act

items.text: PART 1 — the correction
fields: Stopped the act before anything else (Y/N)
Any explaining or justifying at the scene (Y/N — negative)

items.text: PART 2 — the repair
items.teaching_focus: 'Happened at all' is the row that fails most often, and it is the whole drill.

items.text: The crew
fields: What they were told, if anything
What they concluded about the standard
What the officer did to close that loop
Would a probationary member now do the same act
items.teaching_focus: The last question is the only real measure of whether the correction worked.

sources: Self-authored cases, role-player card and rubrics
Department stop-work authority, reporting requirements and discipline thresholds (user-supplied and authoritative)
